# Why Loki is spelled that way — and what it costs to get it right

There is a version of this name the early internet had to settle for: *loki*. This is the file on how **Loki** replaced it.

Loki stands at the center of more Eddic narrative than any figure save Þórr and Óðinn — and almost every road through the mythology crosses him at least once. He is the gods' companion on the road, their rescuer in a pinch, and their ruin in the end: the same wit that recovers Mjǫllnir in Þrymskviða engineers the death of Baldr in Gylfaginning. The Eddas hold both truths without reconciling them, and Skáldskaparmál fixes the verdict in the kenning system itself, where poets are taught to name him the slanderer of the gods. By the giantess Angrboða he is the father of Fenrir, Jǫrmungandr, and Hel; by his wife Sigyn, of Nari and Váli, whose fates are spent in his own binding.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Loki
- **ASCII form:** loki
- **Meaning:** "Possibly knot, loop, or flame"
- **Domain of influence:** Trickery, Chaos, Shape-shifter
- **Pantheon:** Norse
- **Classification:** Tier 2
- **Original script:** ᛚᚢᚴᛁ
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 213 of 406

## The Name Before the Marks


Spoken, the name runs `/ˈlo.ke/` — 'LOH-kee' — two even syllables with the weight on the first; keep the o short and round, and let the second syllable fall away lightly.

## The Temple That Stands Now

The restored name is not a plaque; it is an address. The temple of **Loki** lives at [/loki/](/loki/), with its mythology in the [lore halls](/loki/lore/), its peer-reviewed record in the [Scholarly Edition](/loki/scholars/), and its place in the pattern atlas on the [patterns floor](/loki/patterns/).

One decisive feature survives — a single, honest mark — which places the restoration in Tier-2: exact, and exactly labeled.

## Where the Name Stood First

One carved stone is the entire candidate corpus for Loki's image: the Snaptun stone (Denmark, c. 1000), a hearth-stone or bellows-shield bearing a bearded face with scarred, sewn-shut lips, commonly identified as Loki from the Brokkr episode — an identification widely repeated but unprovable, since the stone carries no inscription. The Kirkby Stephen stone in Cumbria, showing a bound horned figure, has likewise been read as the bound Loki, though scholars also read it as a bound devil of Christian iconography. His attestation is otherwise textual: the Poetic Edda poems survive chiefly in the Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270) and the Hauksbók; Snorri's account is transmitted by the principal Snorra Edda manuscripts (GKS 2367 4to, Codex Wormianus, Codex Upsaliensis). No runic inscription names the god, and no Scandinavian place-name is securely his — a silence that matches his ambiguous cultic standing: the one major god for whom no temple, toponym, or votive deposit is known. The temple on the web is the newest of these addresses — the first one that fits in a pocket.

## The Archetype at Work

The [pattern atlas](/patterns/) seats this temple in **3 industries**, each match argued and weighted: **Disaster Resilience & Recovery** (the bound one whose breaking free opens Ragnarök — the stored-up catastrophe of the northern cosmos.); **Gaming, Fantasy & Entertainment IP** (the trickster archetype entire — from sagas to Marvel, the most-adapted Norse figure in modern fantasy IP.); **Thermal, Geothermal & Fire Energy** (the fire-side companion — fire personified at times, the wildfire that burns what it will.). The [Resonance File](/loki/blog/resonance/) reads those seats through the myths themselves.

The Norse tradition is not a vibe; it is a library. The [Sacred Texts collection](/texts/) holds [Poetic Edda](/texts/poetic-edda/) and [Prose Edda](/texts/prose-edda/) — the primary sources the temple's scholarship is built on. The temple is the argument; the texts are the evidence.
